extracted.intended_audience: NIH investigators, peer reviewers, grant applicants, and research administrators interested in NIH peer review and renewal applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critique about how NIH grant applications (especially competing continuations/renewals and R01s) are evaluated by reviewers and study sections, including score calibration, the role of the Investigator criterion, and how productivity and prior progress are weighed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grants are assessed against each other
rubrics_metrics.description: Grants are assessed against each other in the individual reviewer’s stack and to some extent across the entire study section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How many applications a reviewer has affects pre-discussion calibration of scores; relative ranking within the pile (not absolute quality alone) matters for score assignment and downstream funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score spreading / calibration
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are commonly exhorted to 'spread scores' rather than bunch them up; study sections vary in their calibration of where the hot/critical score zone lies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers and SROs encourage spreading to differentiate applications; the hot zone (often around scores 2–4) is where funding decisions are most sensitive. Percentile attempts to adjust for study-section differences in calibration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer load influences scoring compactness
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of applications assigned to a reviewer (reviewer load) influences how compactly or widely they score applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smaller assigned sets (e.g., three grants) may lead to different spreading behavior than larger, more typical loads (e.g., nine grants). Experimental designs that give reviewers unrealistically few applications risk misrepresenting real-world scoring behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read-phase recalibration
rubrics_metrics.description: After initial scores are nominated and before the study section meets, reviewers commonly recalibrate scores during the read phase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pre-meeting recalibration can shift scores from initial nominations and is an important step in real review practice; omission of this phase in experimental designs is a serious flaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentile as an important funding metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Percentile is a key funding criterion that attempts to adjust for study section differences in score calibration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because study sections vary in scoring distributions and where the 'hot zone' lies, percentile ranking across the study section is often more consequential for funding than raw score alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigator (PI) criterion is central and difficult to fake
rubrics_metrics.description: The Investigator is one of five allegedly co-equal NIH review criteria and the application includes a detailed Biosketch that requires assessment of a specific individual's contributions and history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because reviewer judgments explicitly incorporate the PI’s record, attempts to manipulate perceived PI identity in experiments must overcome reviewers' attention to biosketch details; the Investigator criterion makes faking PI identity in vignette studies especially problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of PI-identity manipulations in experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental manipulations (e.g., changing names to imply race or sex) intended to alter perceived PI identity must be believable and not detectable by reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs must (1) ensure reviewers do not detect deception, (2) debrief and screen thoroughly for detection, and (3) avoid stereotypical cues that don't map to actual PI demographics; inadequate debriefing or allowing reviewers to consult outside resources undermines validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough debriefing and detection screening in reviewer experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies of peer review must robustly identify reviewers who detected manipulations (e.g., fictitious personnel or biosketch lookups) rather than relying solely on self-report mentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple exclusion rules based on whether reviewers 'mentioned' detection are inadequate; explicit, systematic debriefing and questioning (e.g., asking about prior knowledge like Ginther) are needed to assess whether participants were on to the study purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competing continuation (renewal) hinge on past productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Renewal applications are evaluated heavily on the productivity achieved during the prior award; the application must include a Progress Report and list of publications resulting from the prior support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers expect evidence of past output; higher productivity (quantity and impact) strongly favors renewal decisions. Competing continuation review often blends program-level assessment (past performance) with project-level proposed aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glamour publications ('knock our socks off') strongly favor renewal
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptionally high-impact publications or 'Glamour' findings substantially strengthen a renewal application and can outweigh other deficiencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformative or very high-visibility outputs may make reviewers give less weight to strict alignment with prior Aims or exact project match; they can override weaker aspects of the renewal package.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raw productivity matters (number and impact of papers)
rubrics_metrics.description: A respectable number of publications with discernible impact is a crucial credit for a competing continuation; more is generally better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectations vary by field, but reviewers often reward consistent, field-standard publication output. Benchmarks and per-$100k productivity estimates are discussed, but norms vary and multi-award PIs may complicate attribution of papers to a single grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productivity addressing overarching project goals
rubrics_metrics.description: For renewal review, it matters whether publications and outputs relate to the overarching theme of the prior project, not only whether each specific original Aim was completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should explicitly tell reviewers (e.g., in the Progress Report) how outputs map to the broader programmatic goals; reviewers are variably tolerant of divergence from original Aims if the work advances the original overarching objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing original Specific Aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Some reviewers focus tightly on whether the original Specific Aims were addressed; failure to do so can be penalized even if productivity exists elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science naturally evolves, and changing directions can be acceptable, but applicants should justify deviations. Whether addressing every Aim is necessary varies among reviewers and study sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching publications to prior experiments and addressing prior criticisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers may check whether suggested controls or experiments noted in prior summary statements were addressed in resulting publications; omissions can be criticized during renewal review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to address prior recommended experiments or controls (raised in earlier reviews) can be held against the renewal; applicants should explicitly note and explain how prior criticisms were handled or why they were not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior summary statement, score, and percentile affect reviewer judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers of renewal applications see the prior summary statement and past score/percentile, which can influence their evaluation positively or negatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of a previously favorable or unfavorable outcome (including programmatic pickups or ESI-related exceptions) may bias reviewers; panels sometimes debate the fairness of past funding decisions when assessing renewals.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH review mixes project-based and program-based logics
rubrics_metrics.description: Although NIH grants are nominally 'project-based', application materials (Biosketch, prior support, Progress Report) incentivize program-level evaluation of the investigator and past productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers implicitly and explicitly consider both the proposed future project and the investigator's track record; policy proposals to stabilize funding tilt the balance more toward program-based thinking and past performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoffs of stabilizing (program-based) funding versus project-based funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Stabilizing funding for investigators (program-based support) can protect productive labs but risks opportunity cost, stagnation, and reduced flexibility compared to strictly project-based selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy decisions about allocating more program-based funds must balance benefits of continuity (reduced start-stop inefficiency) against risks of supporting 'dead wood' and reducing competition for novel projects.
